:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Simplifying Challenging Expressions Using the Power Rule

:question/problem: Given that  ${a}^{12}=t$ and ${a}^{4}=s$, what is the value of $\frac{{t}^{3}}{s}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we carry out the substitution

$$
\frac{{t}^{3}}{s}=\frac{{({a}^{12})}^{3}}{{a}^{4}}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule followed by the quotient rule 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{({a}^{12})}^{3}}{{a}^{4}} & = \\ \frac{{a}^{12\cdot 3}}{{a}^{4}} & = \\ \frac{{a}^{36}}{{a}^{4}} & = \\ {a}^{36-4} & = \\ {a}^{32}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: For $a>1$, given that ${a}^{9}=t$ and ${a}^{-14}=s$, what is the value of $\frac{{t}^{4}}{s}$?
:question/worked-solution:
First, we carry out the substitution

$$
\frac{{t}^{4}}{s}=\frac{\left({a}^{9}\right)^{4}}{{a}^{-14}}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule followed by the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\left({a}^{9}\right)^{4}}{{a}^{-14}} &= \frac{a^{9\cdot 4}}{{a}^{-14}} \\ &= \frac{{a}^{36}}{{a}^{-14}} \\ &= a^{36-(-14)} \\ &= {a}^{50}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/_canonical-example.:knowledge-point/title: Simplifying Challenging Expressions Using the Power Rule

:question/problem: If $\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{x}}\right)^4 \cdot x = x^k$ for some constant $k$, then what is the value of $k?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we convert the radical to a fractional exponent, and then we apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{x}})}^{4}\cdot x & = \\ {(\frac{1}{{x}^{1/3}})}^{4}\cdot x & = \\ {({x}^{-1/3})}^{4}\cdot x & = \\ {x}^{(-1/3)\cdot (4)}\cdot x & = \\ {x}^{-4/3}\cdot x & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we apply the product rule, adding the exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-4/3}\cdot x & = \\ {x}^{-4/3}\cdot {x}^{1} & = \\ {x}^{-4/3+1} & = \\ {x}^{-4/3+3/3} & = \\ {x}^{-1/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $k=-\dfrac{1}{3}.$
